<reason>PRO framed the decisive question early (the state-protected perpetrator gap) and kept the debate anchored there, using CON's own concessions ("can sometimes overcome obstruction," "successor government," "may be defensible domestically") to show CON's alternatives either collapse into ecocide-by-another-name or leave the incumbent leader untouchable. PRO's Q1 was the sharpest pressure of the debate and CON's answer (specified conduct vs. balancing test) reduced its case to a definitional quibble rather than an argument against international recognition. CON did real damage with the permit "which is it?" dilemma and the correct point that stripping immunity is not the same as establishing jurisdiction over a non-consenting state's domestic conduct, and PRO's "shielding state does not have to accept anything" and "never answered" (before CON's turn) were overreaches. But PRO's recklessness/manslaughter framing adequately answered the demand for a planner's formula, and CON never supplied a tool that reaches the head of state burning his own forest. PRO's closing crystallized the choice more cleanly; CON's remained largely a demand for proof rather than a competing affirmative vision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1/[B4.3] exchange: asking how CON's "negotiated cross-border jurisdiction for precisely defined environmental offenses" differs from ecocide except in name, and which tool reaches a head of state burning his own forest. CON's A1 conceded only a successor government could prosecute, which PRO's closing turned into "waiting for the perpetrator to lose"—the most damaging moment for CON's live route.</best_rebuttal>
